newsitem.title: USA: AEP seeks narrow federal utility legislation.
newsitem.headline: AEP seeks narrow federal utility legislation.

text.p: Federal legislation relating to electric industry restructuring should be clearly defined and relatively narrow giving individual states key authority, American Electric Power Co Inc chief executive E. Linn Draper Jr said Friday.

"The 105th Congress will be very quickly out of the starting gate with electricity restructuring proposals," Draper said. "I would like to think the federal legislation that comes to pass will be of a 'minimalist' variety."
Draper made his remarks as a panelist at "The Energy Daily's" 24th annual conference.

Although American Electric serves seven states and could potentially face seven different timetables for deregulation, Draper would not like to see federal imposition of a blanket deadline for competition on all of the states.

"Federal legislation relating to electric industry restructuring should be narrowly confined," he said. "It should, first, ensure that there is reciprocity among the states. Second, it must effectively address any roadblocks to a level playing field for all power suppliers in a competitive market."

"However, if the states create a patchwork of policies that are incompatible with effective operation of the electric utility system, we would then advocate appropriate federal action to achieve a reasonable degree of uniformity," he said.
Draper also touched on the need for repeal of the Public Utilities Holding Company Act of 1935 (PUHCA) and the Public Utility Regulatory Policy Act of 1978 (PURPA).
"Repeal of PUHCA is necessary to remove the operating restrictions it places on public utility holding companies," Draper said.
"The act has long since outlived its usefulness. It has become a regulatory anachronism, and a barrier to competition and innovation."
PUHCA restricts public utility holding companies geographically, AEP pointed out in a statement.

It also restricts diversification into other lines of business, "a restriction that can eliminate business opportunities that make good financial sense and could save money for customers," Draper said.

PURPA was initially passed to stimulate the development of alternate energy supplies, including cogeneration and renewable energy. Some states required utilities to sign long-term contracts for energy far above the current cost of generation, AEP noted.
Draper cautioned against implementing legislation to enforce a "one size fits all" approach to stranded costs.
"The recovery of stranded commitments should occur during a transition period when rates would be fixed based on state regulatory decisions," Draper said.

"During this transition, utilities would take steps to achieve and to retain cost savings. These savings would be used to reduce the stranded commitments. "At the end of the transition period, full competition would commence with no further protections for generation assets."
Draper objected to recent efforts to require amendments to the Clean Air Act as a prerequisite to electric industry restructuring and the advent of customer choice.
"There is unfortunately a whole campaign of electricity competition versus the environment that has arisen or, more correctly, seems to have been invented," Draper said.
"I refer of course to those complaints from utilities and others in the northeastern states that increased competitive power sales will worsen their pollution problems.

"I simply do not believe that deregulation, competition, and customer choice are in any way inconsistent with environmental excellence. It is well worth reminding ourselves also that utilities have historically tended not just to meet but to exceed what is needed for environmental compliance."
Draper said the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the states have sufficient legal authority to regulate emissions based on sound scientific determination of need.
